newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe army, police battle red locust swarms.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe army, police battle red locust swarms.

text.p: Army and police units have joined an intense fight against invading swarms of red locusts in Zimbabwe which local farmers want to wipe out before the start of a new cropping season late next month.

The country's Commercial Farmers Union (CFU) and the government Agricultural Extension Services (Agritex) said on Wednesday the army and the police had agreed to use their radios and communications to track the red locusts.

"We have used some military helicopters for spraying...and when we met the senior officers, both from the police and the army, they pledged to help us track the locusts," senior Agritex officer Dumisani Nyoni told reporters.
"That is helping our cause. The idea is to hit the locusts very hard wherever they are found, because we don't want them anywhere in this country, especially in the last half of November," he added.
The red locust swarms invaded Zimbabwe from neighbouring Mozambique in August, mostly hitting districts in the south and east of the agriculture-based southern African country.

The CFU said crop damage had so far been minimal, and confined mostly to winter irrigated crops, grass and leaves because the invasion came after the end of the 1995/96 (November-April) cropping season.
But farmers across Zimbabwe have stepped up battles against the remaining swarms ahead of the new season.

As well as ground spraying, the commercial farmers and Agritex have deployed planes to spray the red locusts. CFU entomologist Di Taylor said she believed the insects would be eliminated before new crops were planted.
"There are intense efforts...and no talk of how they (the red locusts) may affect the coming crops. Nobody is talking about losing this fight," she said.
Nature also seems to be siding with the farmers. Some red locusts are reportedly starving to death in Zimbabwe's dry southern Matabeleland province due to a lack of green plants to feed on.
